title: Attentive Kernel Sentinel: seqlen- and architecture-aware autotuner for prefill/decode bursts
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Build a lightweight, production-safe kernel selection controller ("Sentinel") that dynamically chooses attention and compute kernels based on: GPU architecture fingerprint, observed sequence-length distribution per route, token-phase (prefill vs decode), and short-term burstiness. The controller should prefer high-throughput kernels for long prefill batches, low-latency kernels for short decode bursts, and automatically revert to conservative safe kernels if safety bounds are violated.
background: Current runtime uses a static mapping of kernels by model and a few hand-tuned heuristics. We see latency outliers when traffic mixes long prefill requests with short decode bursts on heterogeneous fleet (A100 vs H100 vs L4). Previous autotuners focus on per-epoch offline profiling; we need an online, low-overhead autotuner that reacts to distribution shifts without destabilizing latency SLOs.
objective: Reduce 95th percentile latency on mixed prefill/decode workloads by 15-25% for targeted models, while maintaining or improving average token cost. Provide an experiment framework and dashboard to validate kernel choices and regressions.
success_metrics: p95 latency reduction for mixed workload routes >= 15%
no increase in customer error rate or token-level cost > 5%
ability to safely rollback or quarantine kernel variants within 5 minutes
proposal: Implement a two-tier Sentinelsystem: 1) an online lightweight scorer that uses streaming stats (seq length histogram, recent latency samples, occupancy footprint) to compute a kernel suitability score; 2) a short-horizon multi-armed bandit (Thompson sampling with safety constraints) that explores promising kernels for a route-or-host while enforcing a conservative safety baseline. Safety baseline is a verified kernel chosen by offline validation per GPU family.
design_notes:
Key design choices and rationale:
- Feature inputs: per-route seqlen histogram (5 buckets), token-phase tag (prefill/decode), GPU arch label, recent latency quantiles, and per-kernel probe history. These are compact to keep memory overhead low.
- Decision frequency: decisions evaluated at route-level every 30s and per-host warmstart when new kernel candidates are discovered.
- Exploration cadence: capped trials (max 1% traffic for any new kernel candidate, burst-limited).
- Fail-safe: rollback trigger when p95 increases by >20% vs baseline over a 5-minute sliding window.
- Instrumentation: tag every decision with trace-id and kernel-id for offline analysis and causal attribution.
implementation_plan_tasks: Prototype scorer service (Go) that ingests runtime telemetry and exposes per-route kernel scores
Integrate scorer into runtime routing path with a non-blocking decision cache
Implement bandit trial harness in runtime with traffic capping and safety checks
Add SDK hooks to annotate requests with token-phase and route metadata
Create microbench harness to run candidate kernels under representative seqlen buckets
Add dashboards (Datadog/Grafana) with kernel decision heatmaps and regression alerts
End-to-end QA: synthetic mixed workload replay + shadowing for 48h
Rollout plan: canary on a small fleet, 24h observation, progressive ramp to full fleet

tradeoffs: Exploration vs SLO risk: limiting exploration reduces potential wins but preserves latency SLOs. We bias towards conservative exploration with fast rollback.
Statefulness vs stateless runtime: keeping per-route state enables faster adaptation but increases memory at scale. Chosen compromise: route-level cached decisions with TTL and compact histograms.
Offline profiling vs online adaptation: offline gives stable baseline but misses distribution shifts. We combine both: offline baseline + online trials.
